speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion concerning an extremely urgent matter.
Since the retail price of fluid milk will be raised to 51 cents a quart as of March 1, 1975, which represents a considerable increase in expenditures for large families; considering that between October 1973 and January 1975, the government paid $109 million in grants for the consumption of fluid milk and that this amount represents an
increase in the purchasing power of consumers amounting to $7.3 million a month; considering that inflation more particularly affects large families with low or average income; considering that this action would be beneficial to the consumers as well as to farm producers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That this House ask without debate to the Minister of Agriculture to undertake immediate negotiations with the provincial governments to come to an agreement on the re-establishment of the subsidy on fluid milk and to suggest thereafter to the federal cabinet that a 10 cents rebate or subsidy a quart be applied on the consumption of fluid milk.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Since a number of civil servants who speak both English and French, but who have been classified as unilingual and who are in positions classified as unilingual, are compelled to serve Canadian taxpayers in both official languages, without having their particular ability duly

recognized, which comment applies also to others, with the exception of House of Commons employees, who are not entitled to the bilingualism bonus, in spite of their knowledge of both official languages and ability to serve Canadian taxpayers in both official languages; and since such a situation is unfair to these civil servants, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert);
That the House look into the possible granting of the bilingualism bonus to all civil servants who successfully complete the public service bilingualism tests, so that all civil servants who went to the trouble of learning both official languages and can serve Canadian taxpayers in both languages may be rewarded for their special ability.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION OF ADVERTISING OF MODEL HAND GUNS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my motion under Standing Order 43 is brief and to the point. I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. I do so because of the urgent and pressing necessity of investigating or controlling the advertising of hand guns as contained in an advertisement in the Trail Times of Friday, February 14th, 1975. That date was Valentine's Day, a day which is significant in the history of crime. The advertisement shows four different pistols and two different revolvers of known type and make and states that they are precision machined metal models which look, feel, weigh and even disassemble like the originals. They are perfectly legal. They cannot be fired. Even dummy cartridges are available.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the national concern about the increase in crime and violence and the concern of the government for the control of hand guns, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander):
That the Minister of Justice immediately investigate and act upon this form of advertising.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: DISAPPEARANCE OF PREFERENTIAL INTEREST RATE FOR SMALL BUSINESSES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Finance who will recall that he associated himself, at least, with a preferential rate on bank loans to small business substantially below the rate for larger business. I have received a complaint that this preferential rate for small business has quietly disappeared. Can the minister indicate whether this is so, and whether the disappearance or abolition of this preferential rate for small businesses carries his approval?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: DISAPPEARANCE OF PREFERENTIAL INTEREST RATE FOR SMALL BUSINESSES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when interest rates were going up I asked the banks to consider a preferential rate for small business, which they did. As the interest rates continued to go up, that differential between the prime rate and the prime rate for small business of course increased at the same time. As interest rates come down, that differential diminishes, and I see nothing abnormal in that.

subsubtopic: DISAPPEARANCE OF PREFERENTIAL INTEREST RATE FOR SMALL BUSINESSES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Do I take it from what the minister says that he approves of the disappearance of this preferential rate for small business at the banks? If this is the case, may I ask the minister what the difference is in the present situation compared with the time when this two tier system was introduced with the encouragement of the minister? At that time, in May of 1973, the prime rate was, I think, two full percentage points less than it is today.

subsubtopic: DISAPPEARANCE OF PREFERENTIAL INTEREST RATE FOR SMALL BUSINESSES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the peak of interest rates the differential between the small business loan rate and the prime rate for other business was anywhere from 114 to 1 Vi points. As the rate comes down, that differential diminishes. The fact that that differential is diminishing in no way lessens my feeling, which I have conveyed to the banks, that they ought to continue to give preference in their credit allocation to Canadian-owned small business across the country, as well as to farmers, fishermen and to those areas of the country less reasonably favoured by economic circumstances.

subtopic: INTEREST RATE ON CONSUMER CREDIT-POSSIBLE MAINTENANCE OF RATE TO CONTROL VOLUME

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INTEREST RATE ON CONSUMER CREDIT-POSSIBLE MAINTENANCE OF RATE TO CONTROL VOLUME
speechtext:
One further supplementary, Mr. Speaker. The minister does not make it clear that the two tier system is, in fact, being preserved. Perhaps I might ask him a question about interest rates on consumer loans which seem to have held steady in spite of the reductions in the prime rate. I would like to ask the minister whether this is something approved as an appropriate method of containing the growth of consumer credit. Is it government policy or the policy of his department to encourage the banks to maintain the same level of interest rates on consumer credit
Oral Questions
from the point of view of containing the volume of that credit?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: INTEREST RATE ON CONSUMER CREDIT-POSSIBLE MAINTENANCE OF RATE TO CONTROL VOLUME
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, it is not government policy or the policy of the Bank of Canada to restrict consumer credit, particularly in view of slackening demand in durables in this country. But the hon. gentleman, if he looks over the figures as they developed over 1974 and into 1975, will recall that while the prime rate went up 4 points, the consumer credit on a contractual basis went up only about 1 to 114 points. In other words, the consumer loan rate moved up far more slowly, and it will move more slowly down. The prime rate will be reflected not only in mortgage rates but in consumer rates and other rates as the reduction works its way through the system.

CONSUMER LOANS-SUGGESTION MINISTER INSTRUCT BANKS TO LOWER INTEREST RATES
speechtext: In view of the fact that prime rates have now declined to about 9 per cent and that consumer rates have not fallen correspondingly, may I ask whether the minister has been in contact with the banks instructing or asking them to lower consumer rates, and if not, whether he intends to do so?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: CONSUMER LOANS-SUGGESTION MINISTER INSTRUCT BANKS TO LOWER INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
In my
conversations on a weekly basis with the governor of the Bank of Canada I conveyed this submission to the banks but, as I told the Leader of the Opposition, the consumer rates did not move up to nearly the same extent as the bank rate and other prime rates did-when interest rates moved four points, the consumer rate moved one point up. As the interest rate structure embraces the whole of the rate structure, I think one can assume that the differential between the consumer rates and the prime rate will again readjust.

subtopic: MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES-POSSIBLE LEGISLATIVE ACTION TO CONTROL
MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES-POSSIBLE LEGISLATIVE ACTION TO CONTROL
speechtext:
Has the minister spoken to the banks about mortgage rates? Can he tell us at what level he wants the banks to set mortgage rates.

Oral Questions
If the banks fail to act quickly enough to bring down mortgage rates and consumer rates, bearing in mind their important bearing on inflation and unemployment does he propose to take legislative action to control interest rates in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES-POSSIBLE LEGISLATIVE ACTION TO CONTROL
speechtext: Mortgage interest rates have softened by between one and a half and one and three-quarter points in the last month and a half, reflecting the total movement of interest rates. The specific answer to the hon. member's question is, no. We do not intend to legislate mortgage interest rates. We are interested not only in a reasonable rate for the potential home owner; we also want to ensure a reasonable rate which will attract the amount of money into the mortgage market which, of itself, will have the effect of reducing mortgage rates.

subsubtopic: GRANTING OF BONUS TO ALL QUALIFIED BILINGUAL EMPLOYEES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the President of the Treasury Board.
In view of the fact that there is trouble in the federal public service, in view also of the motion moved earlier by my colleague, the hon. member for Rimouski, relating to a bonus for bilingual federal public servants, and finally in view of the fact that the minister declared recently that only the employees related to Parliament, like secretaries, were entitled to the 7 per cent bonus if they were bilingual, does the minister not agree that we should extend this 7 per cent bonus to all the federal public servants throughout Canada? As it is French-speaking employees object to speaking English in federal offices, and Englishspeaking employees object to speaking French. In my opinion, this 7 per cent bonus would settle those conflicts in all the provinces of Canada. Does the minister intend to do something along these lines?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (President of Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: GRANTING OF BONUS TO ALL QUALIFIED BILINGUAL EMPLOYEES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am aware of this problem. It is extremely

complex, as I told the House of Commons last week. We are now reviewing this situation. The 7 per cent bonus has been instituted because of particular circumstances, because of the fact that the supply of and demand for secretaries did not favour the government. We have been forced to add an extra bonus to find bilingual secretaries, but we do not intend to extend this principle to all public servants. Besides, in relation to the current problem in Montreal, we are reviewing it and we hope to find a solution acceptable to everybody.

subsubtopic: GRANTING OF BONUS TO ALL QUALIFIED BILINGUAL EMPLOYEES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. Does the minister know whether, in Montreal, those who are against the use of the French language are asking for the 7 per cent bonus? I am wondering if the minister admitted yesterday that federal civil servants had the right to strike. Is the matter of the 7 per cent bonus now being looked into by the negotiating committee which has been meeting, after a fashion, day after day, far too long?

subsubtopic: GRANTING OF BONUS TO ALL QUALIFIED BILINGUAL EMPLOYEES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is confusing two situations. The blue collar workers' strike has nothing to do with the bilingualism problem.
With regard to the situation at Montreal and bilingualism, the workers are not on strike but working to rule. I trust the employees concerned will realize that they are not improving the situation by so doing. They should co-operate. We will try to find an acceptable solution.

subsubtopic: GRANTING OF BONUS TO ALL QUALIFIED BILINGUAL EMPLOYEES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask one last supplementary question.
Would the minister tell the House whether it is true that the Unemployment Insurance Commission has harassed and threatened its employees classified as Francophones who refuse to speak English in the performance of their duties, as reported in an article published in Le Jour, which is not my favorite newspaper? Is the minister aware that Unemployment Insurance Commission officials are alleged to have threatened some employees?

subsubtopic: GRANTING OF BONUS TO ALL QUALIFIED BILINGUAL EMPLOYEES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I know nothing about those threats, Mr. Speaker. The Unemployment Insurance Commission tries to give the services all Canadians living in the Montreal area are entitled to. Francophones as well as Anglophones must be dealt with in the official language of their choice. I trust the employees will understand that creating such difficulties does not improve the climate.

Questions addressed to Ministers should relate to the public affairs with which they are officially connected, to proceedings pending in Parliament, or to any matter of administration for which the Minister is responsible. Within these lines an explanation can be sought regarding the intentions of the Government, but not an expression of opinion upon matters of policy.

subsubtopic: MR. NOWLAN-SUGGESTED REFERENCE OF PROCEDURES DURING ROUTINE PROCEEDINGS TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, as I indicated earlier, to raise a question of privilege resulting from the alleged question of privilege raised by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Reid). I will be very brief. I am glad I waited until after the question period to raise my question of privilege which is basically directed at the rights of hon. members.
My question of privilege relates to the incredible performance, outlining in graphic form the distorted parliamentary priorities of the government, in name, but which has yet to show any purpose, direction or conviction about the basic problems of this land. If ever there was a parliamentary example of the ship of state wallowing in a sea of indecision, charting a course on a false compass and without a captain at the helm, yesterday's alleged question of privilege by the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader was it. In relation to the other pressing problems facing this country, it makes one wonder whether in fact there is a government House leader; or is he just a loss leader, discharging his duty to his philosopher king captain to make this institution completely inane and irrelevant so that members can really be nobodies and the machinery and machinations of the Prime Minister's office can have full sway?
What other explanation is there for making the floor of the House of Commons the washroom of the nation as the government, perverting privilege, attempts to muzzle one of its own members by washing its political linen in public. Surely, Your Honour, if permission of the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council is required before an hon. member is allowed to appear before the Senate, then an invidious precedent will be established. Not only will all forms of future privilege be relevant, but we may even have to ask his blessing for the absolutions of the day-especially if it is in a Senate washroom.
As for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre indulging in this parliamentary hoax to generate more wind in his assault on a sterile Senate, the best that can be said is that rarely has an individual been so blinded by the amber light at the crossroads of parliamentary rules that he fails to see that red and green lights control the flow of traffic. His time, as with other House leaders, might more usefully have been spent in raising a valid question of privilege affecting this House in the present paradox of this Parliament of Canada having television in one of its parts even though the whole has made no decision on the matter, notwithstanding the fact that reform of the rules and television coverage were high priority items in the
Privilege-Mr. Nowlan
Speech from the Throne many lost moons ago. Of course, the fact that the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization has not even met in a substantive way to discuss the matter is not, I suspect, a matter of parliamentary privilege but just another example of the ineptitude of this government in the management of its own affairs, let alone meeting the responsibility of the mandate it received albeit by masquerade and misrepresentation.
The only privilege at issue yesterday was the insult to hon. members who convened to discharge public business and were exposed to a sideshow over which they had no control and the people of Canada had no concern. Let us get on with parliamentary business, and not the who, when, where and how this government lost its grit.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall):
That the matter of the question period and the priority and placement of other routine proceedings be referred forthwith to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization with instructions to report back before Easter so that the House can maintain and develop relevant rules for this incompetent government.

Order, please. The hon. member earlier gave the Chair notice of his intention to move this motion pursuant to a question of privilege. I am sure the hon. member will realize that the question is very much one for debate and very much a topical subject relating to the priorities which ought to be given to daily routine business and the question period. The fact that the matter was so quickly referred, after the hon. member's intervention last week, to the standing committee will enable that committee, with a very wide reference-in effect, a blanket reference on the procedures of the House-to begin work at once, which would include the recommendation contained in the motion.
I say that not because of the redundancy and repetitiveness involved, but the fact is that there is machinery already at work which through the regular channels is empowered to do what the hon. member has in mind. For that reason, since at the present time routine proceedings take place before the question period and this is sometimes an inconvenience, this matter is certainly worthy of examination. But the fact is that it is in conformity with the rules and as long as those rules are being enforced I cannot regard it as a question of privilege.
I do, of course, accept it in the spirit in which it is intended, that is, urging that committee to see if there is consensus to experiment with other ways of ordering our priorities. I am sure that all of us are comforted by the blanket order of reference which gives the committee authority to start that work at once.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
When the committee rose last evening, clause 4 as amended was under consideration, the amendment having been proposed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain.
On clause 4.

When we adjourned the debate last night we were discussing the amendment by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain to clause 4 of Bill C-49.1 had commended this amendment to the minister for his serious consideration and requested that he pay special attention to the three speeches which preceded mine last evening. In his speech the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain proposed his amendment. Also in the course of his remarks the hon. member identified far superior fiscal policies and legislative actions which could be followed to achieve the goal of reasonable revenue-sharing between governments and maintain a healthy and viable resource sector in our economy.
The hon. member for Don Valley indicated that it is absolutely unnecessary for the government to proceed with the kind of measures included in clause 4. The hon. member for Peace River indicated that indeed it is very dangerous to the economy of the country, to confederation and to national unity for the government to continue to pursue the line of reasoning it is now following.
I would like very briefly to review the history of the development of the energy confrontation which currently exists, not from the point of view of rubbing salt into old wounds but from the point of view of attempting to identify the lessons which are to be learned. The day this issue began to grow into national proportions can be explicitly identified as September 4, 1973, when the cabinet, after a Labour Day weekend meeting, felt that it must introduce a measure to demonstrate, primarily to the then leader of the New Democratic Party, that it was fighting inflation and it was going to do something to impose a freeze on the price of domestic crude oil produced in western Canada.

This, I might add, came after two other moves by the government that summer to control inflation: price controls on wheat and beef. Wheat, beef and oil were the three commodities on which the government attempted to impose price controls, the three major commodities of importance to western Canada. The reason is quite obvious: this allowed the government the maximum political benefit and the minimum political damage. The fact that this ploy worked is the major reason behind the suggestion by the hon. member for Peace River last evening that it is time we had a renegotiation of confederation. The fact that this so-called national party could get away with alienating that part of the country in the manner it did is evidence that it is time we looked into the whole question of renegotiating confederation, because if some attention is not paid to that matter in the near future, I and many other sincere, concerned Canadians worry about the direction in which this confederation might go.
However, as a result of that unilateral move by the government on that day the producing provinces reacted. This being the third such move, they felt they had to protect their economic interests and they reacted with legislation to protect those interests. The federal government reacted to that legislation; the provincial governments reacted again; the federal government reacted again, and the escalation grew and grew and became very heated until the agreement of March 27 at 24 Sussex Drive when it appeared as if, finally, a solution had been reached. Instead, the government showed that it had no intention of acting in good faith. It acted in a manner which my leader has described as deceitful-this was an accurate description-in introducing the budget of May 6 which merely increased the tensions within the country.
What is the situation in the oil industry? There is now substantial evidence that Canada will be a net importer of oil in the near future. There will be shortages of oil, yet there is no reason why this should be so since Canada is a petrolific country. The net result will be a slowing down of development and an increasing rate of unemployment. These losses to the economy cannot be immediately recouped.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources enjoys taking occasional potshots, along with the NDP, at the multinational companies. In fact, though, the companies most affected by the government's tax policies are the Canadian independent companies which have been doing most of the drilling in the west. Much concern has been expressed by the Canadian government in the past about the need to encourage and preserve Canadian ownership, but no such concern has been shown when it comes to adopting policies which hurt the small portion of the industry where Canadian content is most in evidence. The need to rely on imports of foreign oil in the future will probably result in balance of payments problems, a serious state of affairs. I notice, Mr. Chairman, that you about to rise. I shall have to seek the floor at a later date to complete my remarks.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday we read that the Minister of Finance is shortly going to the Middle East in his capacity as chairman of the interim committee of the

International Monetary Fund to talk about oil, oil production and the reinvestment of profits by oil producing nations. This gives me a point of entry at which to begin certain comments I wish to make. At time like this when I look around the committee-the chamber is not well filled-I feel like suggesting to the minister that he and I should repair to our old Sandy Hill haunts since we might be able to get as much accomplished in the course of a private discussion. However, since this must be done in public I intend to advance a serious argument for the minister's consideration.
I have already addressed myself to the energy situation and tried to present arguments based, not on an "Alberta first" but on a "Canada first" position. I intend to ask the minister how he reconciles his position as Minister of Finance, putting through a bill which will be so injurious to the resource producing provinces, with the other position he holds as chairman of the interim committee of the International Monetary Fund? The situation we face with respect to the use and the development of the resources of Canada was put very plainly by Mr. Maurice Strong, formerly in charge of the Canadian International Agency, in his capacity as head of the United Nations environment program. He said:
To put it in its starkest terms, Canadians must face the prospect of having to defend before the world their continued right to exclusive sovereignty over a disproportionate share of the world's territory and its resources ...
What does this mean for Canada? What should we do about it? In my view it means that Canada has a special responsibility for the way in which it manages the disproportionate share of the world's territory, its resources and the natural environment that it commands.
It must regard itself not just as a sovereign owner and possessor of these advantages but in the larger sense as their trustee. It does not mean that Canadians should be denied the benefits of these resources but they must be prepared to share these benefits. "Canada first" cannot mean "Canada only".
The great question which all of us must resolve as we try to steer our way through a world in scientific, technical and cultural explosion is how to bring together the two great themes of modern times, that is, growth, the development of resources for a suffering humanity, along with conservation. These two things must be developed into a national policy. The minister himself in his budget speech of November 18 when he addressed himself to the subject of Canada working toward international co-operation- the concept he personifies as chairman of the IMF committee-had this to say:
Our ability to co-operate will be severely tested, but we see nothing to be gained from policies of confrontation ...
I am deeply troubled by the potential disaster facing many of the poor countries of the world. A number of them can no longer pay for food, fertilizer, fuel and many other essentials. All countries, including Canada, must review their foreign aid programs in the light of these tragic developments.
I wish to recall to the minister the words he himself used, that there is nothing to be gained from policies of confrontation. That sentence was applied to the field of international relationships: surely, though, he would not deny its applicability to the domestic scene. Nevertheless, I suggest the government is determined to put through a bill taxing corporations in a way which disallows their royalty payments to the provinces for income tax purposes, and that this will place us in a situation in which

the regional strength of the country will be greatly hurt, as a result of which our national strength will be impaired, thus leaving Canada in a weakened position when it comes to playing the role we should be playing internationally.
Last week there was a debate on CIDA. I tried to point out that foreign aid as such was not in question; what was important was a restructuring of the world economy along lines which allowed the developing nations to plug themselves in to interprovincial mechanisms of trade, financing and distribution. I take it the hon. gentleman is going to the Middle East to try to put some pressure on the resource producing states to accept their responsibility to help work out satisfactory solutions to present difficulties. Does the minister not think that he is undermining this country's position internationally by perpetuating a policy, as reflected in legislation, which will hurt the resource producing provinces of this country and weaken their own development?
What about Alberta? We know that 85 per cent of Canada's oil is produced in Alberta. I think Canada should be in a stronger position to meet international commitments for the sake of a more just world order. Naturally, I speak as an Albertan who recognizes that much of the resource strength of this country, strength which depends on the development of oil and gas, is vested in my province. I think that a bill which will diminish Alberta's capacity to produce oil is a bill which will weaken Canada and Canada's international position. I ask the minister to take these facts into account. As he suggested in his November 18 budget speech, international confrontation will get us nowhere. I suggest that confrontation within our own country will, likewise, get us nowhere. This argument is endless.
What does the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain seek to do? It asks the government not to proclaim a certain part of the bill until after the first ministers' conference. One hopes that that conference will be held in a co-operative and flexible spirit and that pricing as well as the constitutionality of the issue we are dealing with will be discussed. One hopes that debate on the constitutional issue will not have been foreclosed, if I may use that word, by action by the Parliament of Canada resulting in provincial royalties no longer being allowed as tax deductions.
I am arguing that we need more time for Ottawa and the provinces to come to an agreement in a spirit of compromise. Already certain things have been done. The November 18 budget is significantly different in certain respects from the May 6 budget in the area of resource exploitation. The Alberta government has introduced a drawback with respect to provincial royalties. Such moves on both sides reflect a spirit of flexibility, a spirit in which both sides are trying to reach out and compromise. The Syncrude partnership is another illustration of my argument. The deal which has been worked out will be in the best interests not of the people of Alberta alone but the people of all of Canada. Again, I say by so doing our governments are working in a manner which will enable Canada to meet international responsibilities.

My argument for delaying the implementation of certain parts of this bill until after the first ministers have met, which is what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain suggested, is reinforced by what happened recently at the two hour meeting in Calgary when the Prime Minister met Premier Lougheed. I want to recap briefly what took place. The Prime Minister implied at that meeting that crude oil price increases are viewed by the federal government as another factor which will have its effect on conservation of energy supplies. On the matter of incentives to the oil industry, the Prime Minister stood firm on taxation policies now in effect. The federal government, he suggested, does not feel that changes in this policy are required and therefore no change in the deductibility of royalty payments to provinces in computing federal tax would be contemplated. The federal government's position, of course, is reflected in the bill before the committee.
For his part, Mr. Lougheed noted that the discussions had centred on energy, transportation, agriculture and petrochemicals. The premier said, again, that Alberta would not move unilaterally on crude oil price adjustments before the first ministers' conference in April. I ask the committee to note that. He suggested that Alberta maintains the opinion that crude oil prices should move closer to world prices, but just how great the first move will be was not stated. The premier expressed the viewpoint that federal government encouragement for the industry was certainly required. Another concern expressed by the premier dealt with Alberta's potential petrochemical industry. Petrosar, in the premier's opinion, could jeopardize development of a viable petrochemical industry in Alberta.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is not correct.

I bring that opinion to the attention of the minister's colleague and seatmate. What is the significance of the Prime Minister's meeting with Premier Lougheed in Calgary. The significance, I suggest is this: these two leaders have obvious differences of opinion on energy matters relating both to crude oil prices and federal-provincial tax jurisdiction; that is, they have obvious differences on the two central questions, the constitutionality of the federal encroachment on provincial royalties, and prices. As well, the Prime Minister and the Premier expressed a difference of opinion on the degree of progress made thus far in resolving these matters.
Would it not be better for the Minister of Finance to tell the committee that the government is willing not to implement certain parts of this bill so that there can be discussion without prejudice at the first ministers' conference, discussion in a spirit of co-operative partnership and cooperative federalism in order to resolve the difficulties which involve not only the premiers of two provinces but all the people of the country? These words are not meant to be rhetoric. In preparing myself for this debate I studied the report of the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the Constitution, presented in June, 1972. The thrust of that report is this: our constitution needs to be updated and modernized. I will not argue about how that can be done; the minister knows the arguments as well as I do. The thrust of these arguments is that we must not only take into account existing relation-

ships between Ottawa and the provinces; we must also remember the conditions under which the constitution was drawn. By upholding the position which says that the central government is the dominant government vis-a-vis the provinces and that this is the modern reality, the minister is not heeding the thinking which went into the making of the joint committee's report on the constitution.
The speech made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, referred to yesterday by the hon. member for Don Valley when he spoke about what he called the "Hamilton proposal", or the velocity of capital concept, was one of the most exciting speeches I have ever heard in parliament. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain introduced the velocity of capital idea on January 30 and it is an idea of which private industry and governments should take cognizance. I do not say that the minister's budget speech was not exciting, but the speech of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was very exciting. Yet the minister came to the committee yesterday and said, in reply to the hon. member, that he had not proposed the idea to the provincial governments and had not discussed it with private industry but that, yes, he recognized its importance. Perhaps too much has been happening. What I am arguing is that: it is wrong for the minister to take unilateral action and ignore the ideas brought forward by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain.
Yesterday the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain reflected on his ideas for dealing with capitalintensive industry in order to give more money to the owners of the resources, the provinces, and more money to the federal government by sharing the profits of the companies, the equity. At the same time, there will be enough money going to the companies to enable them to continue. Those are some of the large issues at stake now as we consider whether we should move ahead with the implementation of clauses 4 and 7 of Bill C-49.
I want to conclude by repeating for the minister, before he goes abroad, a very interesting story which appeared in the International Economic Survey of the New York Times for January 26. The title is, "The world, as wealth shifts, is shaken by uncertainty". We know there is great uncertainty as to which way we should go to repair some of the global problems. The story concludes with a quotation by John E. Sawyer, an economic historian who has taught, if you please, at both Harvard and Yale. He said:
No society can prosper on a divergent course with reality. There can be no escaping the accelerating pace of change, the fact of interdependency or the inevitability that public processes will govern crucial sectors of activity from now on.
I bet the minister will say "amen" to that quotation. Here is the last sentence:
The challenge will be to keep these processes honest, enlightened and effective.
Does the minister really think that clauses 4 and 7 of Bill C-49 are enlightened with respect to the world conditions we face today? Are they really effective in stimulating resource development in Canada, which is the key to a strengthened Canadian economy, and diversified regional growth so that all parts of this country can plug into


making our country strong? I ask this seriously. Will the minister take a moment to answer my central, dominant question? How can he reconcile his position on clauses 4 and 7 of Bill C-49 with his international responsibilities, going into the IMF, helping to restructure the world economy with justice?
This afternoon, Mr. Chairman, I want to make one last appeal to the minister.
The last one?
Hear, hear!

The Quebec Liberal backbenchers should be very interested in this bill. My purpose in rising is solely to address myself to them and try to persuade them to take a second look at the bill before us. We are talking about one very fundamental issue, namely, how do you divide the resources of this country between the federal government and the provincial governments? We have had a whole history of fighting on clause 4 whereby the government will disallow the deducting of royalties.
Hear, hear!

We have had applause from a British Columbia member and no applause from the Quebec members. I suspect that if the Quebec Liberals were to check with Premier Bourassa and his cabinet, they would find that almost every one of them is opposed to this clause in the bill. They would also find that every premier in this country is opposed to the clause which disallows the deductibility of royalties. Royalties are a bit different from other taxes in the country. Under our constitution the provinces have a right to impose royalties. This is not only with regard to gas and oil; it affects all minerals that we produce such as nickel, gold and potash. Therefore, every province in this country is affected. Disallowing the deducting of royalties as a legitimate expense is like telling a farmer in Quebec or Saskatchewan that he cannot claim municipal taxes as a legitimate expense, or telling someone who rents land from a landlord that he cannot claim the payments made as a legitimate expense.
What will happen if the federal government undercuts the provinces with regard to resource revenue? How much room will there be left for the provinces to develop? There have been a lot of moves in the province of Quebec, in particular, for economic, cultural and social nationalism and, indeed, independence of Quebec as a separate entity and a separate province. If the provincial governments are denied further revenues, the federal government will be playing into that sentiment of alienation in one part of this country against another. If hon. members do not vote for this amendment, they will be making Rene Levesque very happy. He will say that this is another example of the heavy-handedness of Ottawa. All the premiers and all the provinces are opposed to this particular clause.
The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister will not even delay this clause for two months until after the first ministers have had a chance to meet. This is a very reasonable amendment. It says that this House will pass the clauses-and I do not agree with them all-if their proclamation is delayed until the first ministers meet.

That would not be a great sacrifice for this government to make. If the provinces are all opposed, why cannot we wait another two months before putting these clauses into law? They will pass the House of Commons and the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance would have the extra clout at the conference in early April. It would be a sign, signal or symbol of good faith if they were not proclaimed until after the conference. Is that asking too much?
Why is it that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are right and all the premiers are wrong? Is that a demonstration of the divine right of ruling this country which seems to have affected the minds of so many Liberals? I know as a fact that if the Liberals were allowed to stand up in this House and say and do what they believe, many of them would vote for the amendment before us. I speak to many Liberals from Quebec, as well as the hon. member for Nipissing who represents part of northern Ontario. I know they are very concerned about development in their areas. There are also members from the prairies and the maritimes who want more development in their regions. However, we cannot have that development without a spirit of co-operation, consensus and working together as a team rather than pitting one region against another.
I have always believed we should have a strong central government. However, if we are to have that it must be with the co-operation of all regions and all provinces. In order to have a strong central government, there must be a certain amount of decentralization with regard to decision-making on issues important to the various provinces and regions. That is what we need if we are to keep Canada together. For too long there has been development around the golden horseshoe, particularly the Toronto area, to the detriment of other regions. A bill such as the one before us will only escalate that type of development instead of narrowing regional disparity.
Yesterday information was provided to me and my colleagues in caucus about recent increase in freight rates. The premier of my province and the premiers of other provinces said they would be willing to give a little more in terms of oil and gas revenues if they could get a little more in terms of some of the things they want, settlement of the grievances they have in confederation.
One thing that grieve us in western Canada is a freight rates system that discriminates against people on the prairies. The same is true for the people in northern Ontario, parts of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. The people of Saskatchewan are providing low-cost oil to people in other parts of the country, generating tremendous revenue for the federal treasury. What do we get in return, Mr. Chairman? I have here the latest figures showing the increase in freight rates and I should like to give the committee two examples of how the freight rate system discriminates against the province of Saskatchewan.
If you ship 610 pounds of meat from Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, to Hudson Bay-not a long distance, only some 200 miles-the cost under the old rates a few days ago would have been $21.80, or $3.57 per hundredweight. A couple of days ago the freight rates went up to $5.40 per hundredweight, representing an increase of 52 per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I have been very patient in listening to this debate for some time, but I cannot for the life of me see how freight rates enter into Bill C-49. I should like to have this debate continue on Bill C-49; I am sure we will be able to discuss freight rates at some other time.

Mr. Chairman, I will tell you why freight rates are very relevant. The province of Saskatchewan produces 75 million to 80 million barrels of oil per year. We have only about ten years' supply of oil left in the province. In good faith the province of Saskatchewan agreed to sell oil to Canadians at a lower price and to export oil to the United States at a lower price, thus allowing the federal government to collect an export tax. As a result, the people of Saskatchewan are losing $5.20 per barrel of oil. They sell their oil at $5.20 below the international price. If that is multiplied by 75 million barrels, it means $400 million per year is being lost by the province of Saskatchewan which would not be lost if the oil was sold at world prices or the export tax was channelled back to the province.
The premier and the people of Saskatchewan have agreed to live with this situation. They are making a substantial contribution to confederation in order to keep down the price of oil and to preserve national unity. In return for this, we expect a trade-off, a quid pro quo. We have grievances against the present transportation structure in this country, against the present freight rate structure and the lack of an industrial strategy. If we had action on those fronts we would be much more willing to allow this clause to pass, but we see no evidence of action. Freight rates have increased over the last two days on commodities that affect the people in the small towns, villages, cities and farms of Saskatchewan. In some cases the freight rates have increased 52 per cent, in other cases 99 per cent or even more.
At the same time, the committee is expecting me to vote approval of a clause that is going to take away more money from the people I represent, and I cannot acquiesce to that. If the Minister of Transport were to tell the House that he will remove the anomalies in our freight rate and transportation systems so as to give the people of Saskatchewan a chance to process food and develop the resources of the province, then I would be willing to compromise and accommodate the government when it comes to gas and oil. Gas and oil don't grow on trees and in ten years' time there will be none left. Then where will we be in the province of Saskatchewan? The federal government and consumers of Canada have taken half our money and we have nothing to show for it.
This clause is vitally important to the province of Saskatchewan and to many other areas of the country which at the present time are underdeveloped. Members of all parties should pay attention to this fact and should ask the Minister of Finance to be reasonable and delay proclamation of these clauses until after the first ministers' meeting. That is not asking him to do very much. He still has

the club, the sanction and seal of the House that the legislation will become law whenever he or the cabinet decide to proclaim it. But this would be a gesture of good will on his part and the whole country would be the better for it, including the Minister of Finance and the government he happens to represent. This country must be built on co-operation and honest intentions. If the minister took this action it would go a long way toward improving the spirit of confederation.
There are many other items in the bill that interest me as a private member. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands and the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie yesterday raised several questions on Syncrude. We all know the Syncrude project has been exempted from many tax provisions made in the last few years. But we want the Minister of Finance to answer these questions as fully as he can and to tell us how much of a concession in terms of taxes will be given to the Syncrude consortium. This is a vital issue at this time. I think the members of the Liberal party sitting opposite should be very concerned at the great sell-out of the oil sands in Alberta to a private concern. This project is being financed by public risk money without any guarantee of profit. Canadians are going to pay the world price for this oil. Costs are skyrocketing and we have little information and very few facts to estimate what the project is going to cost the Canadian people.
I resume my seat after appealing to the Minister of Finance, and particularly to the Liberal backbenchers to show a bit of spunk, to show that they are not puppets on a string who are sitting here in case there is a vote. I ask them to show courage and to tell their minister that the opposition parties on this side of the House are making a reasonable suggestion, namely, that we will pass the bill but delay proclamation of the clauses pertaining to royalties, mineral resources and gas and oil until after the first ministers meeting. I assure hon. members that their own provincial politicians would support them. They do not have very many in Alberta, but I see the hon. member from Battleford-Kindersley is here, and he is from Saskatchewan. I ask them to vote with the opposition and to support our proposition. The Premier of Saskatchewan has been willing to accommodate the federal government, so I would ask them to compromise.
Most of us in our party would like the amendment to go even further. We would like to see these clauses delayed until after the first ministers' meeting or even brought back to the House in a separate bill, but in the spirit of national unity, co-operation and good will we are willing to compromise. We will go halfway and I hope my friends on the other side of the committee will meet us halfway. If they do, it will be better for all of us and there will be political kudos for no one but the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I want to complete the remarks that I started the other day when these clauses were allowed to stand. I want to refer to one sentence in the minister's speech on second reading of the bill in which he said that the issue is; what constitutes a fair sharing of revenue from petroleum and mining as between the industries, the provinces and the federal government?
I do not disagree with that; that is certainly one of the issues, if not the issue. I have yet to hear a case made by


the minister or anybody else on the government side to justify or support the suggestion that the federal government is not getting a fair share. There may be some argument as to what constitutes a fair share, but that has to be sorted out between the federal government and the provinces. The federal government is now getting, and I submit will continue to get, a fair share of these revenues.
Let me refer to some figures I have regarding the federal government's share, on a per barrel basis, of crude oil from Saskatchewan. These figures indicate that the federal government is doing fine in respect of getting a fair share. Medium crude from southeastern Saskatchewan that is exported to the United States, sells at $10.62 a barrel. The federal government's share of that in royalties and federal corporation tax amounts to 58.1 per cent. That is substantially over half. Surely not even the minister would try to tell me that is not a reasonable or a fair share. In fact, I have yet to hear what he would consider to be a fair share in light of figures like that. Since half the crude oil produced in Saskatchewan goes to the United States, that is a pretty significant share, I would submit. Out of the $10.62, the province of Saskatchewan gets 31 per cent in royalties and income tax and the industry gets 5.1 per cent.
In addition, the Saskatchewan government has made available for some period of time an additional 30 cents per barrel to the industry, provided it is used for further exploration and development. Just a few days ago the government improved that position even more by increasing the figure to 50 cents a barrel. That money comes out of Saskatchewan's share of these oil revenues. That gives the producer additional funds. Surely the basic issue is a fair sharing of that revenue between those three groups, the federal government, the province and the industry. Surely that is more than fair.
In addition, the government of Saskatchewan has lived up to its side of the agreement or bargain. As others have said, it agreed to forgo in the neighbourhood of $400 million in revenue that could have been the province's in respect of oil sold at world prices. The government of Saskatchewan was willing to forgo that as a contribution toward equity for all Canadians and as a contribution toward confederation and national unity. That was evidence for the federal government that the province of Saskatchewan cares about a strong confederation and a united country. I suggest that is a good contribution by the people of Saskatchewan from the resources that are theirs under the constitution. I do not want to brag overly about the people of Saskatchewan, but they are the best in Canada and this is a very significant contribution.
The people of Alberta were also willing to forgo in the order of three or four times that amount of potential revenue for the sake of confederation, accommodation and mutual agreement. Saskatchewan and Alberta have lived up to the bargain. These additional revenues which Saskatchewan obtained from royalties were set aside in a capital fund to be used for exploration and development of resources.
I just do not understand what the minister is complaining about or why he found it necessary to put this kind of
Income Tax
measure in the budget. I could understand it if the government of Saskatchewan took that money into general revenue and started to spend it on roads, health care or even for political purposes: I could understand the minister feeling that some measure such as this was necessary because Saskatchewan would then have broken its part of the bargain. It did not do that, but lived up to its bargain to the letter. To get kicked in the face by these clauses in the budget, I submit, is no contribution on the part of the federal government toward confederation, national unity or, for that matter, toward future agreements.
The industry has been claiming it has not been getting enough of the revenue, but there is nothing new about that. It is quite true that until 1958 the industry in Saskatchewan put more into the industry than it took out, but since 1958 there have been increasing net cash outflows from Saskatchewan each year. In 1972 the industry had a net cash outflow of $96.5 million, and in 1973 a net cash outflow of $126.8 million.
From December, 1972, to December, 1973, the price of crude increased by 90 cents a barrel, or 35 per cent, and almost all of that increase went to the producers. Because of events in the Arab countries it was apparent that the price of crude was going to increase at a dramatic rate and that prospect gave rise to legislation in Saskatchewan. It also gave rise to the export tax levied by the federal government, 40 cents a barrel to begin with. I will not go over the whole history of this-I have pages of it here in chronological order-but I suggest if one looked at the whole picture one would not understand why the minister is so excited about this and feels it necessary to have this kind of clause in the income tax bill.
At the end of last March the provincial premiers left a first ministers' conference believing that the taxing agreement in respect of oil would be observed until the end of June, 1974. Certainly no one spoke about tax changes at that conference. The Premier of Saskatchewan wrote to the Prime Minister asking specifically if the federal government intended to disallow the royalties paid to the provinces by the oil producers as a deductible expense when calculating income tax. The Prime Minister did not answer the question at the conference and at no time has he answered it in writing. No wonder all of us in Saskatchewan, at least, were shocked when the budget proposals of May indeed disallowed royalty payments to the provinces as deductible expenses. The people in the industry were shocked. This move came without warning.
We also find it passing strange that the minister is not consistent in how the law will be applied. I still think he is a fair man, although at times unreasonable, but I cannot understand why he does not apply the law in the same way in all cases. If this is such a good idea and is so necessary, then why are royalties paid to private owners such as Canadian Pacific Investments and Hudson's Bay still allowed as deductible expenses when calculating income tax, yet not allowed when paid to the provinces?
Canadian Pacific Investments hold acres of mineral rights in Saskatchewan and lease some of those rights to PanCanadian Oils. PanCanadian Oils can deduct the royalties they pay Canadian Pacific Investments as an


Income Tax
expense when computing their income tax. PanCanadian Oils is a subsidiary of Canadian Pacific Investments, which is a subsidiary of CPR. The CPR can benefit from royalties being deducted as a tax and a subsidiary of CPR can also do so, but not the people of Saskatchewan or the people of Alberta. Surely this is inherently unfair. Surely it is an injustice of the first order.
My first choice, as it is of my colleagues, is that these clauses be left out of the bill now, reintroduced in a separate bill and dealt with as a separate matter after the first ministers' conference. If no agreement can be reached and the government still feels it has to use this kind of measure to get what it thinks is a fair share of the resource revenue, that would be the best way to go about it.
My second choice is to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain. I do not think it is an unreasonable request. So far as I am concerned, it is a minimal request. I hope the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley will agree that it is not all that horrendous a problem to delay the proclamation of these clauses for a couple of months, if for no other reason than to give all the first ministers an opportunity to meet, without rancour, in an effort to reach mutual agreement and understanding, so that the government will not do something which I predict they will regret many years hence and which parliament will regret whatever party happens to be in power.
The legislation which we are considering strikes at a fundamental part of our constitution. It strikes at something that all provinces have held dear since confederation. The opportunity for additional time that this parliament must provide for the federal and provincial governments to reach agreement is one that I hope we will not pass up. I hope that the Minister of Finance will rise in his place and say, "O.K., fellows. I am an agreeable fellow". The provinces have made some concessions. They brought in some measures subsequent to last May 8 to indicate that they are willing to reach an agreement which will benefit the whole country as well as individual parts of it. There have been numerous examples of this, particularly from the premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Surely it is time the federal government responded, if only in this small way, and provided the additional time and opportunity necessary for agreement and understanding to be reached. There may even be time to throw the equalization formula back on the table. The Minister of Finance could say, "Well, fellows; how about doing some adjustment here?" Perhaps he has already done that; I don't know. But surely the couple of months' time that is being asked for is not an unreasonable request. I plead with hon. members from all parts of the country and in all parties to take into account what has been said by myself, by many members of the House and by several provincial governments and I urge them to pass this amendment. I say to my hon. friends on the government side that it will do no irreparable harm to the budget of the Minister of Finance; it will just delay a few parts of it for a couple of months. Since no harm will be done to the budget as a whole or to the government that they support, I hope that hon. members on all sides will support the amendment and bring about the delay for which we and the provinces ask.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking to the amendment proposed to clauses 4 and 7 of Bill C-49 by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, first I would like to say that I recognize the predicament of the provinces and their responsibility for the problem that they generated, particularly my own province. I say that with candour and dismay. But there are limitations to the control which must be exercised in this matter, limitations which are of vital concern to the national interest. After all, the provinces all look to the federal government to provide leadership in developing a fair and just compromise and to re-establish a climate in which employees and employers in the mining industry can continue to contribute to the economy of this country.
The state of the economy of this country is a matter of vital importance to every one of us and certainly to the Minister of Finance. If the minister is to demonstrate his concern for that vast segment of our economy, namely, the mining industry, he will accept the amendment which has been proposed, thereby restoring the faith of the public sector in the industry. I refer to investors in the mining industry.
There is time for further eyeball to eyeball negotiation with the first ministers of the provinces, rather than the confrontation which has generated so much verbiage in the House in the last while. We have been assured by the Minister of Finance, by the NDP, hon. friends to my left, by the NDP in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, as well as by Conservatives in Ontario, that heavy taxation, combined federal and provincial, will not cause existing mining operations to close down prematurely. I heartily agree and so does the mining industry and the Minister of Finance. There is no argument about that. But as sure as blazes there is some argument and some concern about the future.
The Minister of Finance knows, even if some provincial ministers obviously do not, that it takes years and years, and frequently millions of dollars, to prove out a mineral possibility, to establish a mine and to staff the enterprise with miners, engineers, technicians and the necessary equipment. The recent federal and provincial taxes motivated by the higher prices of metals have brought about this greedy confrontation between the provincial and federal governments to the detriment of the entire mining industry and of the people who work in mining areas. Consider the price of copper. Surely the government and the Canadian people recognize that more than any other commodity on the market, the price of metal is subject to major fluctuations, brief high and extended low periods. With rose-coloured glasses they only look at the high prices. This is precisely what was done in the province of British Columbia, and now they are reaping the sick benefits of their political machinations in that regard.
Consider housing in the United States and what it has done to the B.C. lumber industry. Forecast what the same type of thinking and the same trend in the economy, plus federal legislation and provincial legislation, will do to thousands and thousands of men and women who work in the mining industry. This is part of a cycle which the minister proposes to inflict upon British Columbia and miners, smelter workers and all the ancillary services of

the mining and smelting industries. We have already been pilloried and damned by the National Film Board in Trail, and now we are getting this piece of cake served to us. Frankly, we are not at all impressed.
I suspect that the federal government has some sort of death wish for Kootenay West, an area of heavy mining industry, an area of smelting, an area which has provided billions of dollars in taxation for this nation, with nothing in return except this kind of federal legislation to further drive down the economy of this country in general and my riding in particular. I rather suspect that Ontario and Quebec-those two monoliths in the middle of Canada- treat the maritimes, with their coal and iron ore industries, and British Columbia as colonies. When we look at this legislation, what else can we assume?
Canadian mining cannot make an effective contribution to the economy in a climate of this nature. What we must have-and we will not have it unless this amendment is accepted-is the orderly development of the mining community and the mining economy, not cyclical change subject to the whims of provincial and federal ministers, subject to the whims of the marketplace and subject to the whims and economies of other nations with mineral resources and industries. Federal and provincial co-operation is a must. It must be held out to us. The olive branch has been extended and we urge the minister to accept it. Is there any basis in fact for what I have said? The mineral output alone-not the oil or gas output-rose from $475 million in 1946 to $3,278 million in 1969. Production and productivity were up three times the rate of the economy of Canada as a whole. And we are speaking of one industry. What a magnificent achievement and a symbol of industry both for the miners and the mining companies.
There is no evidence on which to assess the short-term and long-term effects of this proposed taxation measure; I think this is the point which disturbs me most. We have yet to hear, from the government side, concrete evidence as to the effects this taxation will have on the mining, oil and gas industries. I ask the minister what the spin-off effects of this particular proposal will be. I urge the minister to tell us what his proposal will do to the mining industry, the oil industry and the gas industry, and what it will do to their employees and to the economy generally. There has not been a word. What is the long-term effect? Has it really been pondered? Has it really been studied? Or has it been popped into a computer for an immediate answer?
Perhaps more than the oil and gas industries, the mining industry needs a long time in order to develop. Capital diverted from the mining industry in Canada is now flowing and will go on flowing to other parts of the world where the same metals are available. Tax and royalty rates in some cases, when we look at the federal and provincial structure of these taxes, reach 100 per cent; yet there is no surprise expressed by or comment from government members at this 100 per cent taxation. I wonder how hon. members opposite would feel if each of them was subject to 100 per cent taxation. There would be a bill before this House pretty damned quick to increase salaries.
I must admonish the minister with reference to the proposal in the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, because the
Income Tax
amendment was submitted with sincerity and integrity as a solution. An hon. member with years of valued experience contributed a valid proposal for the government. Did the Minister of Finance consider it as a solution? No. Did he suggest for a minute that he might invite opinions from the first ministers? Did he ask the mining companies what they thought of the proposal? He could not be bothered; therein lies the shame of the whole thing. It is a valid proposal, developed with sincerity and honesty-and no one bothered with it, least of all the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance has said:
-the federal government should recognize the "special position of the provinces with respect to the taxation and charges on resources within their boundaries"-
That is a strange statement in light of present events, is it not? What did the minister mean by the "special position of the provinces with respect to the taxation and charges on resources"? He meant exactly the opposite of what everyone who read those words thought he meant. He went on:
-the federal government must ensure that provincial royalties, taxes, and other arrangements do not "unreasonably erode" the federal corporate income tax base-
I agree. This has to be part of the discussion between the first ministers of Canada and the Minister of Finance. I agree that some of the mining taxation and royalty proposals of the provincial governments are not conducive to the federal government's receiving its fair share, but I also believe there must be consultation and that any imaginative minister would accept the proposed amendment and at least feed it into the machine for feedback from the provinces and the mining industry. But somewhere along the line the minister's fingers were jammed in the letterbox and the mail was never sent out. The minister also said:
-over-all Canadian tax policy must have regard for the competitive international position of the industry and the financial resources it requires to bring forward production needed in future years.
That is a motherhood statement, if ever I heard one. But what is it doing for us? It might do something if the amendment is accepted; otherwise it is a useless piece of rhetoric and we all know it. If we do not, we should. The fundamental conclusion which can be drawn from the main budget is that the federal government decided it was not prepared to leave taxation and regulation of the resource industries primarily to the provinces. We would accept that, but on the basis of the present proposals how can it possibly be accepted? I know the minister has a bit of a headache over problems in the west, but the west has always been known to generate a headache now and again. Perhaps an olive branch type of aspirin would relieve the headache.
There is little doubt that British Columbia mining royalties were designed to extract as much revenue as possible from the industry as well as to deny a measure of taxation to the federal government. The result is that the B.C. mining companies are placed in the middle of a ham sandwich, a fight between the province and the federal government. The poor mining companies and those who work for them and value their jobs are the ones who are being gobbled up.
